sn11.8:1.3: Verocana, “son of Virocana” is called Bali at [dn20:12.9](). His story is detailed in various legends of later times. He was a great king of the titans who at times even defeated the gods and ruled heaven, but did so justly. Here he seems to have settled his long enmity with Indra.
sn11.8:2.1: Here I’m keeping the masculine forms. they seem to suit Verocana!
sn11.8:2.3: Pali texts read this phrase as either _nipphannasobhano attho_ (nominative singular) or _nipphannasobhino atthā_ (dative singular). I propose both phrases are found, as suits each speaker. The titan Verocana makes a banal assertion and brands it as his own wisdom. The god Sakka improves it by pointing to the cause, echoing [sn11.4:7.3](). This follows the narrative form of Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7–12, where Virocana is easily satisfied with surface teachings, taking only the body to be the Self.
sn11.8:2.4: 8.7.1 has: _prajāpatiḥ iti ha uvāca_, Prajāpati once said
sn11.8:3.4: Indra and Virocana spent 32 years as Prajāpati’s students. Satisfied, Virocana left, while Indra stayed for a total of 101 years.
